title: American AI startups are using Chinese open-weight models in private, they just won't say it publicly
dek: The real moat is not choosing a foundation model—it's fine-tuning open-weight models with proprietary data to build specialized solutions cheaper and more accurate than a giant's single API call.
why: From a startup actually deploying AI, this breaks down the real costs of open-weight versus closed-weight models—more grounded than abstract discussions of ‘distillation’ and ‘benchmarks’. But the ending's speculation about compute and model self-iteration drifts off-topic.
who: Founders and engineering leaders deciding whether to build with closed-weight flagship models or fine-tuned open-weight models, and investors tracking AI infrastructure cost structures.
skip: After 46:09, the ending chat about model self-iteration and AGI speculation drifts off-topic—skip it.

points.h: Use closed-weight flagship models to build, switch to fine-tuned open-weight for production
points.body: Minerva's approach: use cutting-edge closed-weight models like Claude and Astra during development—developer time costs more than tokens, don't waste cycles on loops and errors. Once a task becomes repeatable and needs only "customer satisfaction" quality, switch to a framework with completely different economics: stop measuring by price per million tokens, measure by cost per completed task. That's when open-weight models become your workhorse. This means closed and open aren't substitutes but serve two different economic stages.

points.h: Open-weight models themselves are worthless—the value is in fine-tuning
points.body: According to Daniel, application-layer companies get real value from open-weight models through fine-tuning, not the models themselves. Labs rely on bought massive datasets; startups can't replicate that scale, so they fine-tune on thousands of their own customer data points to specialize a general model. Example: converting user natural-language requests to SQL using OpenAI models was slow and expensive; after fine-tuning Quen, it's faster and more accurate, giving the company a "small advantage"—the logic Harvey and Cognition use when fine-tuning Kimi with proprietary data to build differentiation.

points.h: Cost is the first reason for choosing open-weight, but not the only one
points.body: Daniel ranks enterprise motivations for choosing open-weight models by importance: first is cost—verify that upfront and operating expenses are lower than OpenAI or Anthropic bills. Second is data sovereignty and control: enterprises send data to closed-weight model APIs and get answers, but the model doesn't improve for your use case. Fine-tuning lets the model continuously improve with your data. Third is negotiating power: once you hold "models trained on our own data," you can pressure closed-weight vendors to price by value, not lock you to a single supplier.

points.h: Fine-tuning infrastructure is cheap now, but data quality moats remain
points.body: A year ago, fine-tuning and self-hosting a model needed a full inference engineering team. Now services like Fireworks and Modal let you do it for about 7 to 9 dollars per million tokens in and out; some achieved solid final training for just 90 dollars. Daniel notes Harvey spent roughly 6 million dollars in compute to build its legal Tenant model; now similar work costs "two or three orders of magnitude less." But what hasn't been commodified is data and evaluation system quality—that's the difference between good and bad fine-tuning, and why data companies like Mercor and Surge can charge labs enormous fees.

points.h: The real risk from open-weight models is obliterated models, not data theft
points.body: When preparing this episode, Daniel tested a DeepSeek version with the "refusal" neurons turned off—an obliterated model. It performed near Astra from February this year but costs about 1/100th of Fable. Labs don't actually worry about "China stealing your data." The real threat is anyone tweaking a few parameters to run thousands of PhD-level, zero-guardrail "hacker clones" in the cloud simultaneously—a real security risk happening now, and Daniel admits he hasn't seen a convincing policy solution yet.

points.h: Distillation exists, but Chinese open-weight leadership comes from more than copying
points.body: To the charge that Chinese open-weight models secretly distill from Claude, Daniel offers a counterexample: Reflection AI is a US open-source company backed by Nvidia, running tens of thousands of Blackwell GPUs, strictly following terms of service—yet its flagship model still lags Chinese open-weight models by three to six months. This shows that even with compute and talent and no rule-breaking distillation, you can't keep up with Chinese labs' pace, suggesting distillation isn't the whole story. Chinese labs have made real innovations in sparse model architectures and open-sourced inference frameworks that leading labs have adopted.

points.h: Skip benchmarks—judge open-weight models by whether they handle your daily work
points.body: According to Daniel, benchmarks are almost useless now. A higher score on some benchmark doesn't tell you if it's actually better in real work. His test: can you drop Kimi straight into your existing coding or customer-service workflow and get equal performance? Half-joking, he says the standard is "how often I swear at my terminal"—if that frequency hasn't dropped, the model hasn't caught up yet.

points.h: Every knowledge worker using AI agents will need dedicated GPU compute
points.body: When debating whether compute is enough, Daniel applies first principles: the US has deployed roughly 5 to 10 million top-tier Blackwell GPUs, while knowledge workers number about 100 million. If every knowledge worker gets a full-time agent running 24/7, we'd need far more compute than deployed today. That's why Musk and Huang reportedly found each other at the White House to discuss compute swaps: even the labs themselves face chronic shortages.
